chapter_title: Concerning the Fasting of the Saints
chapter_note: This chapter is entirely institutional/ecclesiastical instruction about fasting practice. While it references substrate cosmological concepts (ruling-power in the body, soul entering through food, darkness-mixture, the Cross, the living soul), these concepts are DEPLOYED to justify fasting — not TAUGHT as cosmic architecture. Both sides of the mapping never stay within the cosmic system: one side is always the institutional practice of fasting by 'the holy man' or 'the saints.' The four-fold enumeration is structured around 'works' of fasting, not cosmic domains or correspondential registers. No extractable oldest-layer teaching exists as a self-standing unit. The chapter represents the compilers' ecclesiastical instruction drawing on cosmological vocabulary that the audience would already know from actual substrate teaching elsewhere.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Pure formulaic opening: 'Once more the enlightener speaks to his disciples.' No cosmological content. Standard dialogue frame attribution.

Introduces the four-fold fasting teaching. 'Saints' (Coptic: ⲛⲉⲧⲟⲩⲁⲁⲃ) and 'fasting' are institutional vocabulary. The four-fold enumeration structure could suggest older patterning, but the topic — 'works' of fasting — is institutional practice, not cosmic architecture. High institutional score (23.08) confirms.

Contains substrate concept ('the entire ruling-power that exists in him' — archontic power within the body, a body-cosmos correspondence). However, this concept is not being taught here; it is assumed and applied to fasting practice. The mapping is practice→cosmic effect ('punish his body by fasting' → 'subdues the ruling-power'), not cosmos→cosmos. The substrate vocabulary (19.05) reflects referenced cosmological concepts, not an extractable teaching unit.

References substrate concepts: soul entering through food, purification from 'the adulteration of the darkness that is mixed in with it.' The darkness-mixture concept is foundational Manichaean cosmology inherited from older traditions. But here it describes what happens when saints fast — mapping practice→cosmic purification, not cosmos→cosmos. The language was composed for this institutional purpose.

References 'the mystery of [the children] of light' — an older cosmological concept. But the paragraph applies it to the fasting person's deeds becoming holy. Heavily damaged by lacunae. Even the recoverable text maps practice→holiness, not cosmic domain→cosmic domain. The phrase 'they live in peace' is devotional closure language.

References 'the Cross' (of Light) and 'the living soul' — both substrate cosmological concepts. But applied to restraining hands from destruction — an ethical/practice instruction. Heavy lacunae make full assessment difficult. Substrate score (9.09) reflects the cosmological vocabulary referenced. 'Restrain their hands' is practical injunction, not cosmic process description.

Recapitulation and summary of the four works of fasting. Entirely institutional: 'profitable to the saints,' 'persist,' 'constant in them daily,' 'make all its members to fast with a holy fast.' No substrate concepts — pure ecclesiastical instruction about practice. Institutional score (7.69) confirms.

Flagged as probable editorial extension by the seam detector — high institutional vocabulary (28.95) with register shift. Addresses those who cannot fast daily, prescribing lord's day fasting and alms. Classic catechumenate-tier instruction: 'their faith and their alms.' This is the latest layer in the chapter, extending institutional teaching with practical accommodation for weaker members. The 'lord's day' reference is a specific institutional calendar marker.
